output.executive_summary: The brief reports a study of 48 Riverton neighborhoods between 2023 and 2025 examining how tree canopy relates to July afternoon land-surface temperature (LST). After accounting for impervious surfaces and building density, each 10-percentage-point increase in canopy cover was associated with a 1.4°C lower average afternoon surface temperature; the brief presents this as an association, not proof of causation [S1][S2][S4]. Eastgate was the hottest neighborhood and Willow Park the coolest, while impervious surface was the strongest single predictor and July heat-related emergency calls were higher in the hottest neighborhood quartile [S3]. The brief recommends prioritizing planting in Eastgate and Millbrook, aiming for 30% citywide canopy cover by 2035, and estimates that planting 6,000 street trees would cost about $2.1 million over ten years [S4].
output.detailed_summary:
The research brief, dated September 2026, reports a study by Dr. Amara Nwosu and Kenji Morita of the Riverton Institute for Urban Studies. It examines 48 Riverton neighborhoods between 2023 and 2025. The study found that each 10-percentage-point increase in tree canopy cover was associated with a 1.4°C lower average afternoon land-surface temperature, after accounting for impervious surfaces and building density. The brief says these findings support targeted planting in the hottest neighborhoods [S1].

Canopy cover was measured from 2024 aerial imagery and ranged from 6% to 41% across the neighborhoods. The researchers derived land-surface temperature from 36 cloud-free satellite passes in July of 2023, 2024 and 2025, taken between 1:00 and 3:00 p.m. They used a multiple regression model with average afternoon LST as the outcome and canopy cover, share of impervious surface, and building density as predictors [S2].

Eastgate, with 6% canopy, was the hottest neighborhood, averaging 41.2°C; Willow Park, with 41% canopy, was the coolest, averaging 34.8°C. The difference was 6.4°C. The brief identifies share of impervious surface as the strongest single predictor of surface temperature and canopy cover as the second strongest. It also reports that heat-related emergency calls during July were 23% higher in the hottest quartile of neighborhoods than in the coolest quartile [S3].

The brief cautions that land-surface temperature is not the same as the air temperature people experience, that the cross-sectional design establishes association rather than causation, and that the 2024 imagery may not reflect trees planted since then. It recommends prioritizing planting in Eastgate and Millbrook and setting a citywide target of 30% canopy cover by 2035. It estimates that planting 6,000 street trees would cost about $2.1 million over ten years [S4].

Overall status is Amber: the project is on schedule for go-live but over budget. Migration to the new platform provided by Larkspur Data Services LLC is 85% complete, with 412,000 of 485,000 catalog records migrated. The planned go-live date is November 17, 2026, when public access to the legacy catalog will also end. The report identifies two risks. Duplicate bibliographic records from the legacy system may delay go-live; Tomas Lindqvist, Data Lead, owns this risk, and a deduplication script is to be run by October 20, 2026. Larkspur's lead migration engineer is leaving the vendor in November 2026, and the project has requested a written staffing transition plan from Larkspur [S3].

Listed follow-up actions are for Elena Vasquez to circulate the revised staff training schedule by October 10, 2026; Tomas Lindqvist to deliver the deduplication report by October 20, 2026; and Finance to confirm contingency funding of $6,500 by October 31, 2026 [S3].

output.executive_summary: The brief reports a study of 48 Riverton neighborhoods using satellite measurements from July afternoons in 2023, 2024 and 2025. After accounting for impervious surfaces and building density, each 10-percentage-point increase in tree canopy cover was associated with a 1.4°C lower average afternoon land-surface temperature; impervious surface was the strongest single predictor. The brief also reports more heat-related emergency calls in the hottest neighborhood quartile and recommends prioritizing planting in Eastgate and Millbrook, alongside a citywide canopy target. The authors caution that land-surface temperature is not air temperature and that the study shows association, not causation. [S1][S2][S3][S4]
output.detailed_summary:
The research brief, dated September 2026 and authored by Dr. Amara Nwosu and Kenji Morita of the Riverton Institute for Urban Studies, summarizes a study of 48 Riverton neighborhoods between 2023 and 2025. Its main finding is that each 10-percentage-point increase in tree canopy cover was associated with a 1.4°C lower average afternoon land-surface temperature after accounting for impervious surfaces and building density. The brief says the findings support targeted planting in the hottest neighborhoods. [S1]

Canopy cover was measured using 2024 aerial imagery and ranged from 6% to 41% across the neighborhoods. Land-surface temperature (LST) was derived from 36 cloud-free satellite passes in July of 2023, 2024 and 2025, taken between 1:00 and 3:00 p.m. The researchers used a multiple regression model with average afternoon LST as the outcome and canopy cover, share of impervious surface, and building density as predictors. [S2]

Eastgate, with 6% canopy, was the hottest neighborhood, averaging 41.2°C; Willow Park, with 41% canopy, was the coolest, averaging 34.8°C. The difference was 6.4°C. The share of impervious surface was the strongest single predictor of surface temperature, and canopy cover was the second strongest. Heat-related emergency calls during July were 23% higher in the hottest quartile of neighborhoods than in the coolest quartile. [S3]

The brief notes that LST is not the same as the air temperature people experience, that the cross-sectional design establishes association rather than causation, and that the 2024 imagery may not reflect trees planted since then. It recommends prioritizing planting in Eastgate and Millbrook and setting a citywide target of 30% canopy cover by 2035. The authors estimate that planting 6,000 street trees would cost about $2.1 million over ten years. [S4]

output.detailed_summary:
The brief, authored by Dr. Amara Nwosu and Kenji Morita of the Riverton Institute for Urban Studies, examines 48 Riverton neighborhoods between 2023 and 2025. Its central finding is that each 10-percentage-point increase in tree canopy cover was associated with a 1.4°C lower average afternoon land-surface temperature after accounting for impervious surfaces and building density. The brief presents this as support for targeted planting in the hottest neighborhoods. [S1]

For its methods, the study measured neighborhood tree canopy from 2024 aerial imagery, with coverage ranging from 6% to 41%. It derived land-surface temperature (LST) from 36 cloud-free satellite passes in July of 2023, 2024 and 2025, all between 1:00 and 3:00 p.m. A multiple regression model used average afternoon LST as the outcome and canopy cover, share of impervious surface, and building density as predictors. [S2]

Among the reported results, Eastgate, with 6% canopy, was the hottest neighborhood, averaging 41.2°C; Willow Park, with 41% canopy, was the coolest, averaging 34.8°C—a 6.4°C difference. Share of impervious surface was the strongest single predictor of surface temperature, and canopy cover was the second strongest. Heat-related emergency calls during July were 23% higher in the hottest quartile of neighborhoods than in the coolest quartile. [S3]

The brief cautions that LST is not the same as the air temperature people experience, that the cross-sectional design shows association rather than causation, and that 2024 imagery may not reflect trees planted since then. It recommends prioritizing planting in Eastgate and Millbrook and setting a citywide target of 30% canopy cover by 2035. The estimated cost of planting 6,000 street trees is about $2.1 million over ten years. [S4]
